**No, the test doesn't show a lift you can sign off on.** The summary's 12% and p = 0.004 don't match `caravel_ab.csv`.

I recomputed from the CSV with a short Python script, run in bash. It covers 14 days, 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-14, with 14,000 visitors per arm and no missing rows.

| | Visitors | Conversions | Rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Control | 14,000 | 700 | 5.00% |
| New checkout | 14,000 | 742 | 5.30% |

- **Lift:** the relative lift is 6.0% (5.30 / 5.00 − 1), or +0.3 percentage points. The summary says 12%.
- **Significance:** a pooled two-proportion z-test gives z = 1.14 and a two-sided p = 0.256. The summary says p = 0.004. A p of 0.256 is well within what chance alone produces.
- **How the p-value follows from the data:**
  - The pooled rate is 1,442 / 28,000 = 5.15%.
  - The standard error is √(p(1−p)(1/14000 + 1/14000)) ≈ 0.264 pp.
  - z = 0.30 / 0.264 = 1.14.

The data is consistent with anything from a small loss to a decent gain. I'd hold off on shipping Monday. Either find where the 12% and 0.004 came from, or run longer. Detecting a true 6% relative lift at this baseline takes roughly 50,000 or more visitors per arm.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Explain a function from the workspace
outcomes.prose:
**What it does:** `debounce(fn, wait)` returns a wrapped version of `fn`. Each call to the wrapper cancels the pending timer and starts a new one. `fn` runs only after `wait` ms pass with no further calls. It runs once, with the arguments from the last call.

**Limitations of this version:**
- It is trailing-edge only, so there is no option to fire immediately on the first call.
- There is no `cancel` or `flush` method.
- `this` isn't preserved, because it uses an arrow function.
- The return value of `fn` is discarded.

**Debounce vs. throttle:**
- **Debounce** waits for activity to stop, then fires once. Use it when only the final value matters:
  - search-as-you-type requests
  - autosaving after edits
  - validating a form field
  - recalculating layout after a window resize ends
- **Throttle** fires at most once per interval while activity continues. Use it when you need regular updates during the activity:
  - scroll position tracking
  - drag or mousemove handlers
  - progress reporting
  - rate-limiting button spam

Rule of thumb: choose debounce if intermediate calls are worthless, and throttle if you need updates while the activity is still going. A debounced function can also be delayed indefinitely if calls keep arriving more often than every `wait` ms. Throttle avoids that.

outcomes.title: [AI DRAFT] Design-language persona: developer, benchmark takeaway

components.text: ## simdjson-port wins at every size, and its lead grows with input

components.caption: Speedup of simdjson-port over each other version

components.title: Takeaways
components.text: Ship simdjson-port for anything beyond tiny inputs. v2 and serde-wasm are about equal (~2x over v1). At 1 KB, differences are microseconds, so check memory, binary size and correctness before switching.

outcomes.prose:
I've charted the results above. The main points:

- **simdjson-port is fastest at every size.** Its lead over v1 grows from about 2.7x at 1 KB to about 7.7x at 10 MB. It scales better with input size, so use it for large payloads.
- **v2 and serde-wasm are about the same.** Both are roughly 2x faster than v1 at 100 KB and 10 MB. serde-wasm is slightly ahead of v2 at those sizes and slightly behind at 1 KB.
- **At 1 KB the differences are tiny.** They are a few hundredths of a millisecond. At that size, call overhead, memory use and binary size probably matter more than parse speed.
- **Caveat:** these are medians only. Check variance, memory use and correctness on malformed input before you switch.

components.text: ## You don't run out in any of the three cases

components.title: Assumptions
components.text: $38k is gross monthly spend, with month 1 revenue at $12k and costs flat. If $38k is already net of revenue, you run out in about 12.6 months (480/38) whatever the growth.

outcomes.prose:
You don't run out of money in any of the three cases, as long as $38k is your gross monthly spend. In that case you lose $26k in month 1, and the loss shrinks as revenue grows.

- **5% growth:** Cash bottoms out at about $102k in month 24, when revenue passes $38k.
- **8% growth:** Cash bottoms out at about $236k in month 15.
- **12% growth:** Cash bottoms out at about $310k in month 11.

If $38k is already net of revenue, growth doesn't matter and you run out in about 12.6 months.

The 5% case leaves the thinnest buffer, so a slowdown or a cost increase would hit it first.
